hook: Every AI app re-invents tool connections. MCP — the Model Context Protocol — ends that: **one open standard to plug models into tools and data. USB-C for AI.**

scenes.title: The N×M problem: N apps × M tools, hand-wired forever
scenes.narration: Before MCP, every integration was bespoke: your app talked to Slack one way, to Jira another, to your database a third — and every OTHER AI app repeated the same work. N applications times M tools equals N-times-M custom integrations, each with its own auth, schema drift, and maintenance burden. MCP — Model Context Protocol, open-sourced by Anthropic in late 2024 — solves it the way USB-C solved chargers: a single protocol defining how an AI application DISCOVERS and CALLS capabilities exposed by a server. Build an MCP server for your system once, and every MCP-speaking host — Claude Desktop, IDEs, agent frameworks, your own apps — can use it. The ecosystem bet: write tools as MCP servers, plug them anywhere.

items.s: Discovery, schemas, calls, results — standardized; no bespoke per-app wiring
Filesystem, GitHub, database servers exist — your app consumes them without custom code
Servers expose curated capabilities — the app never gets raw database credentials

scenes.narration: The third point is architecturally underrated. Without MCP, giving an agent database access often means handing over a connection string — the agent can run ANY query. An MCP server sits in between: it exposes 'search-customers' and 'get-order' as named, described, validated tools — AG-02's discipline enforced at a protocol boundary. The app sees tools; the credentials stay inside the server. That's a security architecture, not just a convenience. And the reuse compounds: reference servers for filesystem, GitHub, Postgres, Slack ship maintained; you configure, not build. The pragmatic mental model: MCP is to tools what REST was to HTTP services — a convention that made integration composable.

scenes.title: Three roles: **host, client, server**
scenes.sub: Who asks, who connects, who serves
scenes.narration: MCP splits the world into three roles. The HOST is the AI application the user interacts with — Claude Desktop, an IDE, your agent. The SERVER is the thing that OWNS capabilities: it wraps a database, a SaaS API, a filesystem, and exposes tools, resources, and prompts. Between them sits the CLIENT — one per server, created and owned BY the host; the host speaks MCP to each server through its client. The rule that keeps it clean: hosts initiate; servers never call the host unprompted. One host can hold many clients — your IDE might simultaneously connect to a filesystem server, a GitHub server and a database server — each an independent MCP connection with its own capabilities and permissions.

layers.s: The AI app · owns the LLM, the conversation, the UX · creates clients
Carry the MCP protocol · capability discovery · call routing
Filesystem · GitHub · database · your internal systems · expose curated capabilities

scenes.narration: Read the arrows' direction: host initiates everything; servers respond. The host asks each server at connect time: 'what do you offer?' — the server returns its capability lists: tool names with schemas, resource URIs, prompt templates. The host presents these to the model — the tool list becomes the function-calling schema — and when the model chooses a tool, the host's client routes the call. This discovery step is the protocol's quiet superpower: capabilities are declared, not hard-coded — a server upgrade adding a tool appears in the model's menu without any host-side change. AG-02's lesson applies verbatim: those discovered descriptions are what the model reads when choosing.

scenes.title: Three primitives: **tools, resources, prompts**
scenes.narration: MCP standardizes three capability types, distinguished by who controls them. TOOLS: model-controlled actions — callable functions with schemas; the model decides to invoke them mid-conversation. RESOURCES: app-controlled data — addressable content identified by URI: files, database records, API responses; the APPLICATION decides which resources enter context — often with the user's selection — not the model; resources are data, not actions. PROMPTS: user-controlled templates — reusable prompt patterns the server offers; the user picks them, typically from a menu. The clean mental model: tools DO things, resources ARE things, prompts SAY things — keep the three roles separate and the protocol stays predictable.

cards.s: Data, app-curated · URIs like file:///docs/a.md · "here is context"
Templates, user-selected · reusable workflows · "say it this way"

scenes.narration: A filesystem server illustrates all three: tools — read-file, write-file — model-invoked actions; resources — the file tree, each file a URI the app can attach to context; prompts — 'summarize this directory', a template the user triggers. The control split matters for safety: if MODELS could pull arbitrary resources, every data exfiltration worry of agents would apply to reading too; app-controlled means a human or host policy decides what data enters the window — you saw this pattern in AG-03's file tools, now standardized. When designing your own server: default to resources for anything read-only and data-shaped, tools for anything with side effects, and resist making data-fetching a tool — that's what resources are for.

scenes.title: stdio vs HTTP — and what MCP adds over plain function calling
scenes.narration: Two transports carry MCP. STDIO: server runs as a local subprocess; the host speaks JSON-RPC over standard input and output — the default for local tools on your machine, simple and fast. HTTP — streamable HTTP: the server runs remotely, reachable over the network, enabling shared team servers and SaaS capabilities — this replaced the earlier HTTP-plus-SSE design as the spec matured. Now the fair question: models already have function calling — what does MCP ADD? Function calling is a MODEL-level mechanism: you define schemas per request. MCP is an APPLICATION-level protocol: standardized discovery — hosts learn a server's capabilities at connect time, standardized lifecycle, multi-server composition, and an ecosystem of reusable servers. Function calling is the assembly language inside; MCP is the plugin standard around it.

items.s: Subprocess, stdin/stdout JSON-RPC · personal tools, zero deployment
Network-reachable servers · shared team/enterprise capabilities, needs auth (AG-07)
Discovery, lifecycle, multi-server composition, reusable ecosystem — the protocol AROUND the calls

scenes.narration: When to choose which transport: personal, machine-local capabilities — filesystem helpers, local scripts — stdio, because zero deployment beats everything for solo tooling. Team-shared or cloud capabilities — a CRM bridge, an internal search server — HTTP, because one deployed server serves every host in the organization, and now you're operating a real service: authentication, versioning, observability — AG-07 and AG-08 cover that operational life. The composition point deserves a last word: because servers are uniform, the host can merge tool menus from many servers, handle name collisions, and apply consistent permission policy across all of them — cross-cutting concerns solved once at the protocol layer instead of per integration. That's the N-times-M collapse in action.

scenes.title: Concepts in hand. The spec itself is evolving — catch up.

recap: MCP = open standard replacing N×M bespoke integrations; servers expose curated capabilities behind a trust boundary
Three roles: host (initiates), client (per-server connection), server (owns capabilities, discovered at connect time)
Primitives: tools (model-invoked actions), resources (app-curated data), prompts (user-selected templates); stdio for local, HTTP for shared

quiz.q: In MCP, who initiates connections and calls?
opts: The host always initiates; servers respond — servers never call the host unprompted
quiz.why: Host-initiation keeps control flow predictable and is foundational to the protocol's security posture.

quiz.q: What's the key difference between an MCP tool and an MCP resource?
opts: Tools are model-invoked ACTIONS; resources are app-curated DATA the model doesn't pull directly
Tools use HTTP, resources use stdio
quiz.why: Splitting actions from data — with different controllers — is the protocol's core safety and predictability property.

quiz.q: What does MCP add on top of model function calling?
opts: An application-level protocol: capability discovery, lifecycle, multi-server composition, reusable servers
quiz.why: Function calling is per-request schema plumbing; MCP standardizes discovery, composition and reuse across the whole app.

code.title: Capability discovery: what a server announces
annot: Discovery is declarative: the host needs zero prior knowledge of a server's capabilities
Note the 'NOT for…' clause — description discipline from AG-02 applies verbatim to MCP tools
Resource URIs are just addressing — the host/app decides which ever enter the context window

notes:
# MCP Concepts

## What & why
- N apps × M tools = N×M bespoke integrations. MCP = one open protocol (Anthropic, late 2024).
- Server = trust boundary: curated tools, credentials stay inside.

## Roles
- **Host**: AI app, owns LLM + UX, initiates everything.
- **Client**: one per server, host-owned, carries the protocol.
- **Server**: owns capabilities; announced via discovery at connect.

## Primitives
- **Tools**: model-invoked actions (schemas).
- **Resources**: app-curated data (URIs) — model doesn't pull directly.
- **Prompts**: user-selected templates.

## Transports & comparison
- stdio (local subprocess) vs HTTP (remote/shared, needs auth).
- MCP ≠ function calling: protocol AROUND the calls (discovery, lifecycle, composition, ecosystem).
